definition: Pretending to refuse or not want something you actually desire.
example_1: Oh, I couldn't take the last slice, she said, plate already tilted toward it.
example_2: No, no, the trophy should go to the whole team, he said, gripping it with both hands.
example_3: I never win these raffles anyway, she said, buying eleven tickets.

definition: Driving a point home by piling up phrases that restate and reinforce it.
example_1: The fence failed us: it leaned, it splintered, it let in every rabbit in the county.
example_2: She earned that promotion. She stayed late, she trained the new hires, she saved the autumn launch, she kept the whole floor calm.
example_3: The soup was a triumph, a comfort, a rescue, a warm hand on a cold week.

definition: A composition in which the first letters of successive lines or words spell out a word.
example_1: Her note home spelled HELP down the margin: Having fun. Eating well. Loving camp. Please write.
example_2: The bakery's four specials, read top to bottom, spelled RYE.
example_3: Dad's packing list spelled TENT with its first letters, which is exactly what he forgot.

definition: Exaggeration that declares something so unlikely it is impossible.
example_1: The river will run uphill before that committee agrees on a font.
example_2: I'll finish this inbox when goats file taxes.
example_3: Sooner will the moon rent a rowboat than my sourdough starter survive July.

definition: A story whose surface narrative consistently stands for a second, hidden meaning — characters and events map onto ideas.
example_1: A garden tale where each weed is a bad habit the gardener refuses to name.
example_2: An office story where the broken elevator stands for a rigged promotion ladder.
example_3: Animal Farm reads as barnyard drama on top and political history underneath.

definition: Repetition of the same initial consonant sound across nearby words.
example_1: Seven silver spoons slid silently sideways.
example_2: The bakery's big blue banner buckled in the breeze.
example_3: Grandpa grumbled, grabbed his gloves, and got going.

definition: A brief, unexplained reference to another work, event, or figure the reader is trusted to catch.
example_1: Cleaning that garage was my twelve labors.
example_2: She smiled like she knew where the wardrobe led.
example_3: He met his Waterloo at the spelling bee.

definition: A sentence whose grammar allows two different readings.
example_1: The sign said SLOW CHILDREN AT PLAY, and the kids never let the town forget it.
example_2: She photographed the moose wearing her raincoat, and the paper printed both readings.
example_3: FOR SALE: piano by a woman leaving town with carved oak legs.

definition: Expanding a simple statement with detail after detail to raise its intensity or importance.
example_1: It rained — cold rain, sideways rain, rain that found the gap under the door.
example_2: He was late: late for the bus, late for the meeting, late for the apology.
example_3: The soup was salty — aggressively salty, apologize-to-your-ancestors salty.

definition: A detail placed in the wrong time period, by error or by design.
example_1: In the village pageant, a knight checked his wristwatch before the joust.
example_2: The novel set in 1850 has its heroine skim a paperback that would not exist for a century, and the author knows it.
example_3: The museum diorama of ancient fishermen included, to the curator's horror, a plastic cooler.

definition: Pausing to ask the audience or reader what they would think or do.
example_1: You have seen the leftovers in the office fridge. I ask you: who among us would have labeled them?
example_2: What would you have done, holding the last ticket and hearing the train?
example_3: Neighbors, look at this pothole. Is this the crater of a serious street?

definition: A sentence that breaks off and lurches into a different grammatical track midstream.
example_1: The recipe said to fold the, you know what, we are ordering pizza.
example_2: I was going to explain the budget, but honestly, has anyone seen my calculator?
example_3: So the plan was, and I want credit for the plan, actually the plan no longer matters.

definition: Repeating the last word of one clause as the first word of the next.
example_1: The rain filled the gutters; the gutters fed the barrel; the barrel saved the garden.
example_2: Practice builds habit. Habit builds speed. Speed wins the relay.
example_3: She trusted the map. The map trusted a bridge that was no longer there.

definition: The moment a character discovers the truth about a situation or identity.
example_1: Sorting her late aunt's letters, she recognized her own handwriting on the oldest one.
example_2: The rival baker across the street turned out to be the pen pal he had written to for years.
example_3: Halfway through scolding the dog, she saw the muddy prints were her own boots.

definition: A word or phrase formed by rearranging the letters of another.
example_1: 'Listen' rearranged becomes 'silent.'
example_2: The villain's name, Alma Dun, unscrambles to 'maudlin.'
example_3: 'Dormitory' hides 'dirty room.'

definition: An extended comparison that explains an unfamiliar thing by mapping it onto a familiar one.
example_1: A password manager is a keychain for doors you can't see.
example_2: Editing a draft is pruning a hedge: cut for shape, not out of anger.
example_3: Learning scales is stretching before the run of a song.

definition: Repeating the same word or phrase at the start of successive clauses or sentences.
example_1: We will fix the roof. We will fix the fence. We will fix, at last, the argument about whose turn it is.
example_2: Every morning the ferry horn. Every morning the gulls. Every morning the same seat, saved.
example_3: No map, no flashlight, no idea, and somehow no regrets.

definition: Deliberate inversion of normal word order for emphasis or rhythm.
example_1: Cold was the coffee, and long the meeting.
example_2: Into the basement crept the cat.
example_3: Patient he was not.

definition: A short personal story told to make a point.
example_1: Before explaining budgets, she told about the summer she spent nickels on stickers.
example_2: My uncle opens every toast with the tale of the runaway lawnmower.
example_3: The coach settled the debate with a story about one missed free throw.

definition: Repeating a word so that it carries a different meaning each time.
example_1: If you don't book the flight, we'll have to book it out of here on foot.
example_2: She had a run in her stocking and then a run of bad luck and then, finally, a run to catch the bus.
example_3: Learn to press pause before the deadline starts to press you.

definition: Answering a negative point by attaching a compensating positive one.
example_1: The cabin has no heat, but the blankets are legendary.
example_2: Yes, the car is slow; it is also the only one that starts in January.
example_3: My garden grew one tomato, and it was, in fairness, a magnificent tomato.

definition: Using a word as a different part of speech than usual, such as a noun as a verb.
example_1: Can you calendar me for Thursday before the whole week avalanches?
example_2: He porched the evening away with lemonade and zero apologies.
example_3: Stop adulting for one afternoon and come see the kite festival.

definition: Giving human traits, behavior, or speech to nonhuman things — the thing literally acts human.
example_1: The toaster sulked until Thursday, then forgave us.
example_2: In the film, the moving boxes unionize and demand bubble wrap.
example_3: Our router holds grudges against the microwave.

definition: A deliberate letdown that follows a big buildup, usually for comic effect.
example_1: The vault took three hours to drill open and contained a single expired coupon.
example_2: She trained all year, flew across the country, stepped up to the podium, and read the wrong speech.
example_3: The prophecy foretold a great disruption in the village, which turned out to be roadwork.

definition: Repeating the words of one phrase in reverse order in the next.
example_1: Pack your patience for the trail, and let the trail unpack your patience.
example_2: We shape our tools, and then our tools shape us.
example_3: Do not count your customers before your customers can count on you.

definition: Using a single word ironically to mean its opposite.
example_1: They called the massive mastiff Peanut.
example_2: Here comes Speedy, she said, as the old elevator began its long deliberation.
example_3: The team named the leaky rowboat Unsinkable and kept a bucket aboard.

definition: Setting two opposing ideas in parallel structure to sharpen the contrast.
example_1: Speech is easy; silence is expensive.
example_2: We planned for the flood and drowned in the drought.
example_3: Small keys open big doors.

definition: Substituting a title or descriptive phrase for a proper name, or a name for a type.
example_1: Ask the Spreadsheet Whisperer down the hall; she can fix anything with columns in it.
example_2: The little chef of apartment 4B left cookies on every doormat again.
example_3: Every block has its Scrooge, and ours guards the good parking cone.

definition: A compact, memorable statement of a general truth.
example_1: A borrowed umbrella teaches you about the borrower, not the rain.
example_2: Nobody washes a rental car.
example_3: The list you lose is the list you needed.

definition: Calling into question whether a word truly applies to the thing it names.
example_1: You call this a summer? I have seen warmer refrigerators.
example_2: How can it be a shortcut if we have been walking for an hour?
example_3: That is not a beard; that is a rumor of a beard.

definition: Mentioning something while claiming not to mention it (also called paralipsis or praeteritio).
example_1: I won't bring up who left the gate open, Gerald, because we are past blame.
example_2: Far be it from me to mention that my chili won last year, but the trophy is on the mantel.
example_3: We need not discuss the karaoke incident; this meeting is about the budget.

definition: Expressing doubt, real or staged, about what to say or how to proceed.
example_1: How do I even begin to describe my grandmother's driving?
example_2: Whether to warn the new tenant about the radiator or let the radiator introduce itself, I honestly cannot decide.
example_3: What can be said about a casserole like that? Words feel small.

definition: Breaking off a sentence and leaving it unfinished, the ending implied.
example_1: If your father sees the lawn before we fix it, well.
example_2: The letter began, By the time you read this, and then the ink simply stopped.
example_3: One more scratch on that trailer and I swear I will, you know what, hand me the keys.

definition: Directly addressing an absent person, an abstraction, or an object as if it could hear.
example_1: O patience, where do you go at bath time?
example_2: Dear knees, I apologize in advance for the stairs at the stadium.
example_3: Old house, you kept every secret except the draft under the door.

definition: A name that comically or neatly fits its owner's occupation or nature.
example_1: The town's best plumber was, inevitably, Mr. Waters.
example_2: Nobody was surprised when Sunny Fields opened a flower farm.
example_3: Our dentist, Dr. Paine, insists the sign is working exactly as intended.

definition: Deliberate use of old-fashioned words or phrasing for flavor or effect.
example_1: Hark, the microwave hath finished its labors.
example_2: The invitation read: thou art summoned to the potluck, bring forth thy famous beans.
example_3: Alas, quoth the mechanic, thy alternator is no more.

definition: A recurring character type, image, or pattern that readers recognize across stories.
example_1: The reluctant mentor who says no twice before saying yes.
example_2: The trickster who breaks the rules and accidentally saves everyone.
example_3: The flooded town that must be left behind for the story to start.

definition: A brief remark delivered to the audience that other characters do not hear.
example_1: While the customer studied the menu, the waiter turned to us: the fish, between friends, is a gamble tonight.
example_2: She smiled at the judges, then, sideways to the camera: the cake is entirely frosting.
example_3: As grandfather began the story again, the boy caught our eye: this version adds a bear.

definition: Repetition of vowel sounds within nearby words.
example_1: The June moon soon drooped over the dunes.
example_2: A fleet of green beetles creeped between the reeds.
example_3: Try to light the fire tonight.

definition: Opening with an attention word like listen or behold before the real statement.
example_1: Listen: the ice cream truck changes routes on Fridays.
example_2: Behold, the world's most stubborn jar lid.
example_3: Mark this: the shortcut through the fairground is never shorter.

definition: Dropping conjunctions between clauses or items to quicken the pace.
example_1: We packed, we drove, we forgot the tent.
example_2: The kitchen was chaos: flour, smoke, alarms, laughter.
example_3: He came, he saw, he left early.

definition: A character who asks the questions the audience is silently asking.
example_1: The new intern finally said what we were all thinking: what does this machine actually do?
example_2: In the ghost story, the skeptical cousin demands the rules of the haunting, so the reader learns them too.
example_3: Wait, the rookie said, walk me through how the heist gets past the second door.

definition: A character who serves as the author's stand-in and voices their views.
example_1: The novelist's every book features a weary librarian who lectures the town about reading, and the town suspects who she really is.
example_2: In his comic strip, the artist draws a beleaguered cartoonist whose deadlines match his own to the day.
example_3: The screenwriter added a character whose only job is to sigh at meetings the screenwriter also attends.

definition: The author steps past the story to address the reader directly.
example_1: Reader, I ask you to remember the umbrella; it matters in chapter nine.
example_2: And here, dear reader, you already know more than the detective does.
example_3: Forgive me for pausing the chase, but you should see the map.

definition: The history that happened before the main story, revealed to explain the present.
example_1: She never explains why she checks the lighthouse twice; the old logbook in her drawer does.
example_2: Before the bakery feud, the two owners ran one shop with one oven, and one unpaid debt.
example_3: The scarred workbench came with the house, along with the story of the storm that built it.

definition: An abrupt fall from the lofty to the trivial or ridiculous.
example_1: He vowed to conquer his fears, master his destiny, and finally return his library books.
example_2: The eulogy for the old oak praised its century of shade, its shelter for generations of birds, and its excellent Wi-Fi reflection.
example_3: She sailed for glory, for discovery, for the ages, and for the coupon that expired Sunday.

definition: Seeking guidance by opening a book at random and reading whatever passage appears — as practice or plot device.
example_1: Unable to decide, she let the dictionary fall open and obeyed the first noun.
example_2: Each dawn the captain cut the atlas and sailed toward whatever page turned up.
example_3: He flipped the cookbook for advice and took 'let rest, covered' as a sign.

definition: A coming-of-age novel tracking a protagonist's growth from youth toward maturity.
example_1: Jane Eyre follows an orphan from cold schoolrooms into hard-won selfhood.
example_2: Great Expectations walks Pip from the marshes to London and back to humility.
example_3: A first-generation kid narrates every scholarship form on the way to becoming herself.

definition: An itemized catalog of praise listing the features of a person or thing one by one.
example_1: Her toolbox: hinges of brass, drawers of cedar, a handle worn to the shape of her grip.
example_2: The ode to the diner listed its virtues: the bottomless coffee, the vinyl booths, the pie case lit like a jewelry counter.
example_3: He praised the old bicycle part by part: the bell's clear ring, the basket's woven patience, the tires that forgave every curb.

definition: Opening and closing a work with the same scene, image, or line so the ending echoes the start.
example_1: The story opens with an empty birdcage on the porch and ends with the same cage, door propped wide on purpose.
example_2: Her essay begins and ends at the same bus stop, but by the last paragraph she is the one driving.
example_3: The film's first shot and last shot are the same kitchen table, set for one, then set for six.

definition: A character acknowledges the audience or admits to being inside a story.
example_1: Mid-chase, the thief looked straight out of the page: you saw where the guard went; blink twice for the alley.
example_2: The narrator paused the recipe to admit that chapter three exists only because her editor loves soup.
example_3: Do not worry, the villain told the audience, I am contractually obligated to lose.

definition: Harsh, clashing sounds chosen deliberately to grate the ear.
example_1: The clanking gearbox gnashed, screeched, and choked on grit.
example_2: Crows cracked the dawn with jagged, scraping racket.
example_3: Buckets banged down the back stairs in a clatter of tin.

definition: A deliberate pause or break in the middle of a line of verse.
example_1: I meant to write — the phone rang twice — a shorter poem.
example_2: We buried the time capsule || then forgot the yard.
example_3: Stop here, traveler. Rest. The hill can wait.

definition: Exaggerating a subject's most distinctive traits for comic or critical effect.
example_1: The play's landlord is nothing but a jingling ring of keys and the word no.
example_2: In her sketch, the committee chair is one enormous gavel with a tiny hat.
example_3: The novel's food critic sniffs his water, sends back the ice, and reviews the napkins.

definition: A strained, far-fetched use of a word or metaphor pushed past its normal sense.
example_1: His voice was a rusty hinge singing the furniture apart.
example_2: She drank the whole horizon in one homesick gulp.
example_3: The deadline chewed through the calendar with velvet teeth.

definition: An extended list deployed as a device, letting sheer enumeration carry the meaning.
example_1: The junk drawer held string, batteries, three kinds of tape, a whistle, spare hinges, birthday candles, and the answer to none of our problems.
example_2: Her packing list was a biography: field guides, two harmonicas, dry socks, dried mangoes, a folding saw, and no phone charger.
example_3: The town's lost-and-found ledger read like a poem: one mitten, one trumpet, one ambition, unclaimed.

definition: The methods by which a writer reveals who a character is — through action, speech, thought, appearance, and others' reactions.
example_1: She alphabetized the spice rack in someone else's kitchen; we knew her instantly.
example_2: He answered every question with a question, even 'coffee?'
example_3: The dog liked everyone except Deleon, which told us plenty.

definition: A detail introduced early that must matter before the story ends.
example_1: Chapter one lingers on the spare canoe paddle; chapter nine is a flood.
example_2: The aunt mentions her beekeeping suit exactly once, four scenes before the swarm.
example_3: If the tour guide points out the dumbwaiter, someone is riding it by act three.

definition: A mirrored structure where the second phrase reverses the order of the first.
example_1: Ask not what the garden gives you; ask what you give the garden.
example_2: She sings when she works, and works when she sings.
example_3: Plan your ride, then ride your plan.

definition: Talking around a thing with many words instead of naming it directly.
example_1: He described a 'handheld device for the relocation of soil' rather than say shovel.
example_2: The memo called layoffs 'a rebalancing of human capital allocations.'
example_3: She needed the room where the porcelain furniture lives.

definition: Ending a scene or installment at a moment of unresolved suspense.
example_1: The episode ends as the ferry pulls away with only one of the twins aboard.
example_2: She opened the acceptance letter, read the first line, and the chapter stopped.
example_3: The final page of part one: the doorbell rings, and the dog, for the first time ever, does not bark.

definition: Arranging words or clauses so each ranks higher in force than the last.
example_1: First we lost the trail, then the daylight, then the argument about who had the compass.
example_2: He risked his allowance, then his bicycle, then the whole summer.
example_3: It began as a leak, swelled to a flood, and ended as the lake the town is named for.

definition: Informal, everyday language used deliberately in writing.
example_1: The recipe's last step just said: let it hang out in the fridge a while.
example_2: Y'all can fuss about the paint color after the barn actually has walls.
example_3: The manual for the fancy telescope began, real talk: go outside first.

definition: An elaborate, surprising metaphor sustained and developed across a passage.
example_1: The essay treats her family's group chat as a weather system, with fronts, pressure drops, and one aunt who is entirely lightning.
example_2: For three stanzas the poem insists the public library is a harbor: cards are passports, fines are customs, the atlas shelf is open sea.
example_3: His toast built the marriage as a two-person orchestra, tuning through the lean years toward one long shared downbeat.

definition: The struggle between opposing forces that drives a story — person versus person, self, nature, or system.
example_1: Two sisters want the same empty storefront for different dreams.
example_2: A ranger races a wildfire to a cabin she swore she'd never revisit.
example_3: A clerk fights a form that cannot be completed without the form itself.

definition: The emotional shading a word carries beyond its literal meaning.
example_1: 'Childlike' glows; 'childish' stings; the dictionary can't tell you why.
example_2: Call the house 'cozy' and it sells; call it 'cramped' and it sits.
example_3: 'Thrifty' is a compliment your aunt gives; 'cheap' is one she doesn't.

definition: Repetition of consonant sounds within or at the ends of nearby words, not just at the beginnings.
example_1: The odd lad paddled the flooded road.
example_2: A flock of thick black socks lay stacked on the rack.
example_3: First and last, the lost list mattered most.

definition: A sentence that states its main clause first, then accumulates modifying details afterward.
example_1: The train left on time, hissing at the platform, shrugging off pigeons, carrying our entire brass band and none of the sheet music.
example_2: She planted the flag at the summit, hands raw, laughing at the wind, forty minutes ahead of the record and two hours ahead of her brother.
example_3: The market opened at dawn, canvas stalls blooming one by one, coffee smoke drifting past the fish tables, everyone lying cheerfully about their prices.

definition: Delivering absurd or extreme content in a flat, matter-of-fact tone.
example_1: The goat is on the roof again, she said, refilling her coffee.
example_2: Per the incident report: the piñata retaliated at approximately 3 p.m.
example_3: He noted, without looking up from the crossword, that the canoe had left without them.

definition: Describing something familiar as if seen for the first time, making it strange again.
example_1: The visitor described our handshake ritual: two strangers grip and pump each other's arms to prove neither is holding a weapon or a grudge.
example_2: A toddler's view of the vacuum: the roaring pet that eats the floor and is worshiped weekly.
example_3: The report described toast as bread that has been publicly frightened until it turns brown.

definition: The literal dictionary meaning of a word, stripped of emotional shading.
example_1: 'Snake' denotes a legless reptile, whatever your shiver says.
example_2: Denotatively, 'home' is only a dwelling place.
example_3: 'Cheap' denotes low cost; the sneer is extra.

definition: An abrupt, unearned rescue arriving from outside the story's logic to resolve the plot.
example_1: Just as the lease expired, a never-mentioned aunt willed them the building.
example_2: The dragon has the heroes cornered; lightning solves it in one sentence.
example_3: A drone drops the missing key into the final scene, unexplained.

definition: Repeating a word or phrase with one or two words wedged in between.
example_1: The bridge, the impossible bridge, was finished by June.
example_2: Run, kid, run; the sprinklers wait for no one.
example_3: It was cold, bitterly cold, and the bus shelter had opinions about neither.

definition: Rendering the flavor of regional or local speech in written dialogue.
example_1: The ferryman squinted at the sky and allowed that the fish were biting awful good for a Tuesday.
example_2: Ain't no hill for a climber, Gran said, and took the stairs two at a time.
example_3: That storm's fixin' to sit on us all weekend, the innkeeper said, sliding over the extra quilt.

definition: A writer's deliberate choice of words and register — formal, slangy, clinical, plain.
example_1: The eviction notice said 'vacate'; the neighbor said 'they're putting you out.'
example_2: She wrote 'commence' in the grant and 'kick off' in the group chat.
example_3: The nurse chose 'discomfort'; the patient chose a different word.

definition: Deliberately wandering from the main subject before circling back to it.
example_1: The lecture on knots paused for ten minutes about a ferry mishap in 1962, which, the instructor noted, is why we learn the bowline.
example_2: Before I explain the missing cake, you must understand my brother's history with frosting.
example_3: The trail guide interrupts its own directions to discuss huckleberries, then admits the turnoff was two paragraphs ago.

definition: Explicitly spelling out which sense of a word you mean.
example_1: The cabin is rustic, and by rustic I mean the raccoons have seniority.
example_2: We need this done soon, where soon means before the glue dries, not before winter.
example_3: She said the hike was moderate, moderate meaning you will cry only once.

definition: A double or look-alike of a character, often uncanny, often a foil to their identity.
example_1: The new hire has your name, your handwriting, and better luck.
example_2: A pianist keeps meeting a man booked into every hotel as him.
example_3: Her reflection started waving first.

definition: A phrase engineered to carry a second, slyer meaning alongside the innocent one.
example_1: The bakery's slogan, We Knead You Badly, did double duty on the delivery vans.
example_2: The gym's sign promised: we will make your New Year's resolution work out.
example_3: Her orchard stand advertised: fruit so good, it's pearfect and we cantaloupe without you.

definition: The audience knows something a character does not, and watches them act without it.
example_1: We saw the winning ticket fall behind the dresser; he vacuums the whole scene praising his own luck.
example_2: The reader knows the surprise party waits in the dark kitchen while she rehearses her resignation speech on the porch.
example_3: Every viewer knows the bridge is out; the shortcut argument in the car keeps going anyway.

definition: A sustained speech in which a character reveals themselves to a silent listener.
example_1: For two pages the retiring lighthouse keeper addresses the new bulb, and by the end we know his whole marriage.
example_2: The poem is one side of a barbershop conversation, and the customer's silence tells the rest.
example_3: In her audition piece, a toll collector explains the river to a duckling, confessing everything the river took.

definition: Substituting a harsher, blunter term for a neutral or mild one.
example_1: He calls the community pool the ankle soup.
example_2: Her brother refers to the minivan as the rolling shoebox.
example_3: The crew's name for the office coffee was pipe sealant.

definition: An exclamatory outburst that vents sudden emotion.
example_1: At last! The seventeen-year cicadas, and my new screen door!
example_2: What a catch! And what a terrible moment for the net to be a hat!
example_3: Oh, glorious laundry day, when every sock has a partner!

definition: Writing that vividly describes and responds to another work of art.
example_1: A poem that walks through Hokusai's wave from the rowers' side.
example_2: Two pages spent inside the museum guard's favorite painting.
example_3: A sonnet arguing with the smirk of a thrift-store portrait.

definition: Deliberately omitting words or events, trusting the reader to fill the gap.
example_1: Monday she bought the boat. Friday, the island had a mayor.
example_2: He proposed at the trailhead; the descent, all four hours of it, goes undescribed.
example_3: The minutes read: motion raised, discussion, motion withdrawn, new gavel ordered.

definition: A deliberate grammatical error made for emphasis or voice.
example_1: We was robbed, the whole bleacher section agreed, and grammar could wait.
example_2: Them pancakes ain't going to eat themselves, Grandpa announced, correctly.
example_3: It don't rain forever, she painted on the barn, and the town believed the barn.

definition: A formal, glowing tribute praising a person or thing (also called panegyric).
example_1: The retirement speech crowned the janitor the true principal of the building, keeper of keys and calmer of boilers.
example_2: Her essay praises the humble zipper: uniter of jackets, savior of tents, tiny train on a silver track.
example_3: The newsletter's tribute to the crossing guard ran longer than the mayor's profile, and no one objected.

definition: Running a line of verse past its break so the sentence spills into the next line.
example_1: The poem breaks after 'she packed her whole' and lands on 'garden into one seed envelope.'
example_2: Each line ends mid-promise, so the reader falls into the next: 'I will meet you when the / ice gives up the dock.'
example_3: His verse about the elevator drops its floor between lines: 'we rose past every / thing we meant to say.'

definition: An argument that leaves one premise unstated for the listener to supply.
example_1: Of course the cat did it; the cat was in the room.
example_2: She's a gardener, so the casserole will involve zucchini.
example_3: He owns three ladders. Clearly he can hang one banner.

definition: Beginning and ending a sentence or clause with the same word or phrase.
example_1: The lake gives, and when the fog lifts, you thank the lake.
example_2: Work bought this house, and this house remembers the work.
example_3: Nothing worried her, and she worried about nothing.

definition: Immediately correcting or upgrading what you just said for emphasis (also called correctio).
example_1: The bake sale made hundreds, no, thousands, if we count the pledge from the dentist.
example_2: He walked, sprinted really, to the mailbox every day that week.
example_3: It was a good dog, a great dog, the only dog to hold public office in this county's heart.

definition: A brief, pointed, witty statement, often with a twist at the end.
example_1: The early bird gets the worm, and the late bird gets the coffee shop to itself.
example_2: A shortcut is the longest distance between two points that includes an apology.
example_3: Everyone wants a garden; nobody wants August.

definition: A quotation or motto placed at the head of a work or chapter to set its theme.
example_1: Chapter one opens under a line from an invented almanac: plant nothing you are unwilling to explain.
example_2: The mystery begins with an epigraph from the fictional detective's own field manual: every alibi is a story with a budget.
example_3: Her memoir's first page carries her grandmother's rule, stitched on a real pillow: measure twice, forgive once.

definition: A closing section after the main story ends, showing aftermath or future.
example_1: Ten years later, the bakery is a bank, but the recipe survives on a corkboard.
example_2: The epilogue finds the detective retired, feeding pigeons, still counting them.
example_3: One last letter, dated long after the war, answers the first chapter's question.

definition: A character's sudden, clarifying realization that reframes everything.
example_1: Halfway through alphabetizing his complaints, he realized he simply missed the old crew.
example_2: Watching her daughter feed the parking meter for a stranger, she understood what the allowance had actually taught.
example_3: The chess club's worst player saw it at last: he had been guarding a square nobody wanted.

definition: Telling a story through letters, messages, or documents.
example_1: The whole feud unfolds in laundry-room notes, escalating from 'please' to legal citations to, finally, a shared detergent budget.
example_2: Her novel is told in postcards home, and the lies get smaller as the mountains get bigger.
example_3: The story arrives as a padlocked lost-and-found logbook, one entry at a time, until the entries start answering each other.

definition: Repeating the same word or phrase at the end of successive clauses or sentences.
example_1: The tent leaked at midnight, the boots leaked at dawn, and honestly the whole trip leaked.
example_2: When we were down, she showed up. When the van died, she showed up. Payday or no payday, she showed up.
example_3: He wanted the corner office, deserved the corner office, and got the corner, no office.

definition: A descriptive tag attached to a name or standing in for it.
example_1: Homer's 'rosy-fingered dawn' rises again and again.
example_2: Around here she's simply 'the bridge lady' who saved the crossing.
example_3: Alexander the Great needed no last name.

definition: Repeating a word immediately, with nothing in between, for raw emphasis.
example_1: Stir, stir, stir; custard forgives nothing.
example_2: The gulls found the fries. Run. Run, run, run.
example_3: Quiet, quiet, quiet, the librarian mouthed, pointing at the napping toddler.

definition: Composing a speech in the imagined voice and character of someone else.
example_1: The class assignment: write the lost mitten's account of winter, and she gave it a soldier's stoicism.
example_2: For the anniversary, he wrote a toast in the voice of the couple's ancient hallway clock, which had seen everything.
example_3: The ranger's newsletter runs a column written as the campground's oldest raccoon, worldly and unrepentant.

definition: A sudden joyous turn that snatches a happy ending from certain disaster.
example_1: The orchard was lost to frost, everyone agreed, until the bees found the one warm hollow and the late bloom came in roaring.
example_2: As the auction gavel rose over the family boathouse, the missing deed slid out of the harbormaster's atlas.
example_3: The choir's bus broke down at midnight, and the only tow driver awake turned out to have a spare bus and perfect pitch.

definition: A softened expression substituted for a blunt or unpleasant one.
example_1: The goldfish 'moved to a bigger tank upstairs.'
example_2: The airline 'reaccommodated' half the passengers.
example_3: Grandma is 'resting her eyes' through the whole film.

definition: Smooth, pleasing sound patterns chosen to soothe the ear.
example_1: Low lamplight lulled the mellow room to sleep.
example_2: A murmur of warm water wandered under willows.
example_3: Her lullaby lingered, soft as falling flour.

definition: An ornately balanced, alliterative, elaborately patterned prose style.
example_1: The invitation read: as the moth to the lantern and the tide to the moon, so are the neighbors to a free brunch.
example_2: His apology arrived gilded: not as the storm regrets the fence, but as the fence forgives the storm, do I return your ladder.
example_3: The menu described soup as the summer's surrender, simmered slowly, seasoned with the sighs of sweet onions.

definition: A brief story told to prove or illustrate a moral point.
example_1: To teach the value of checking twice, the foreman tells of the crew that tiled a kitchen for the wrong address.
example_2: Her lecture on patience is one story: the man who dug up his carrots weekly to see how they were doing.
example_3: The coach's parable of the untied shoelace has prevented more falls than any drill.

definition: A short tale, often with animal characters, that lands on a lesson.
example_1: The crow who hoarded shiny things could not fly home ahead of the storm, and the plain-nested sparrow slept dry.
example_2: A hare challenged the ferry to a race across the lake and learned what the tortoise never mentioned: swimming.
example_3: The ant lent the grasshopper a coat, and the moral surprised everyone, including the ant.

definition: Fiction presented in the form of a real artifact such as a report, transcript, or manual.
example_1: The story is a homeowners association newsletter whose bylaws grow stranger until item 14 bans the sea.
example_2: Her novella masquerades as an appliance warranty, exclusions and all, for a machine that grants modest wishes.
example_3: The tale unfolds as a middle school field trip permission slip, amended eleven times, each amendment more alarming.

definition: Breaking the expected grammatical symmetry of a list or pair — a flaw, or a deliberate jolt.
example_1: He liked biking, to fish, and naps — and the sentence limped like his knee.
example_2: The flyer promised fun, food, and that parking would eventually exist.
example_3: She wanted a raise, respect, and to never see the copier again.

definition: Telling the story from inside it, through an 'I' who takes part.
example_1: I counted the lifeboats twice, because nobody else on that ferry seemed interested in arithmetic.
example_2: I did not steal the recipe. I inherited it early, without asking, from a kitchen that was briefly unattended.
example_3: The day I became the town's substitute mail carrier, I learned every dog's opinion of my ankles, personally.

definition: An interruption that returns the narrative to an earlier time.
example_1: Mid-interview, the smell of chalk drops her into a third-grade classroom.
example_2: The chapter breaks from the storm to the summer the dam was built.
example_3: One photograph, and he is nine again, holding the winning ticket.

definition: Jumping ahead to show events from the story's future before returning (also called prolepsis).
example_1: Between innings, the narrator shows us the trophy case twenty years on, one plaque hanging crooked.
example_2: The chapter breaks from the wedding toast to a glimpse of the couple, gray and laughing, arguing over the same map.
example_3: Mid-argument about the seed order, we cut to next autumn: the field is entirely, victoriously, sunflowers.

definition: A character whose contrast highlights another character's qualities.
example_1: The cautious accountant rooms with a skydiving instructor.
example_2: Reckless Laertes makes deliberate Hamlet look even slower to act.
example_3: Her silence gets louder next to her chatty twin.

definition: Early hints that quietly prepare the reader for what's coming.
example_1: The tour guide mentions, twice, that the ice cracks earliest near the boathouse.
example_2: Chapter one lingers on the spare tire nobody checked.
example_3: He waves goodbye from the platform like a man practicing it.

definition: An outer story that introduces and contains an inner story.
example_1: A stranded train car of strangers passes the night trading tales, and the blizzard outside keeps the frame closed.
example_2: The novel opens with a landlady finding a tenant's tape recorder; every chapter after is one cassette.
example_3: At the reunion, the eldest cousin holds up one chipped mug, and the story of the mug becomes the story of the family.

definition: Third-person narration that slips into a character's inner voice without quotation marks.
example_1: Marisol studied the ticket. One seat left, window, of course it was the window, she always drew the window when the mountains were on the other side.
example_2: The dog watched the suitcase come down from the closet. So it was happening again. Fine. Someone had to guard the socks.
example_3: He reread the committee's email. Wonderful, another synergy meeting, because the first nine had been such festivals of progress.

definition: Poetry without a regular meter or rhyme scheme, shaped by breath and emphasis instead.
example_1: Her poem about the laundromat runs long and unrhymed, folding its lines the way the dryers tumble, on no schedule but heat.
example_2: The elegy for the corner store refuses meter; it lists the candy shelf in plain lines and lets the register bell end it.
example_3: His free verse about fog rolls past every expected beat, the way fog ignores fences.

definition: Joking in the face of grim or hopeless circumstances.
example_1: As the flood reached the porch, Grandpa rated the river's punctuality five stars.
example_2: The crew of the sinking dinghy debated whether this counted as a swim or a commute.
example_3: Nice of the storm to prune the orchard for free, she said, over what used to be the fence.

definition: The protagonist's own flaw or error that sets their downfall in motion.
example_1: The champion never practiced returns; her serve was too good to need them, until the final, when it wasn't.
example_2: He trusted every handshake, which built the co-op, and then signed the one that lost it.
example_3: The captain's gift for improvising meant no checklists, and the checklist was where the harbor charts lived.

definition: Expressing one idea through two words joined by 'and' instead of one modified term.
example_1: Come in out of the wind and the weather; the kettle's on.
example_2: He gave the fence a coat of paint and patience.
example_3: She spoke with grace and iron, and the meeting ended on time for once.

definition: Placing words with similar endings near each other so the endings chime.
example_1: The pamphlet promised camping, fishing, whittling, and belonging.
example_2: Rapidly, quietly, expertly, the sisters emptied the cookie tin.
example_3: The job wanted someone dependable, teachable, and unshockable, preferably by Monday.

definition: Excessive pride that invites downfall.
example_1: He skipped the safety briefing; he'd 'sailed worse in his sleep.'
example_2: She framed the rejection letters early, certain the prize was hers.
example_3: Icarus got one instruction and improvised.

definition: A boast disguised as a complaint or as modesty.
example_1: Ugh, my zucchini won again and now I have to store a trophy the size of a canoe.
example_2: It is honestly exhausting being the only one whose sourdough rises every single time.
example_3: So embarrassing: the marathon photographers only got shots of me passing people.

definition: Attaching a descriptive word to a nearby noun instead of the one it logically fits (also called transferred epithet).
example_1: She spent a sleepless pillow of a night before the results.
example_2: He lit a nervous cigarette on the courthouse steps.
example_3: We ate a triumphant breakfast the morning the well finally ran clear.

definition: Scrambling normal word order, beyond simple inversion, for dramatic effect.
example_1: Strange, the mercy of strangers is.
example_2: Him I trusted; the paperwork, never.
example_3: Uphill, in August, barefoot, went the parade anyway.

definition: Deliberate exaggeration for emphasis or humor, not meant literally.
example_1: I've told you a million times to preheat the oven.
example_2: Her suitcase weighed as much as a small moon.
example_3: The line at the bakery wrapped around the calendar.

definition: Asking a question and then immediately answering it yourself.
example_1: What does a lighthouse keeper actually do all winter? Mostly, he counts kinds of silence.
example_2: Why does the market open at dawn? Because the fish keep fish hours, and fish are not negotiators.
example_3: Who fixed the churn before the fair? The same aunt who fixes everything, on the condition nobody watches.

definition: Building sentences from ranked, subordinated clauses that show how ideas depend on each other.
example_1: Because the pass froze early, and since the mules refused the lower trail, which the spring flood had gnawed thin, the mail waited a week.
example_2: Although she had promised to sell the piano, which had crossed two oceans before she was born, the first offer made her hide the key.
example_3: When the tide finally turned, after the nets were mended and before anyone dared say the word luck, the boats went out together.

definition: Reversing the natural order of events to put the more important one first.
example_1: Let us win the cup and enter the tournament!
example_2: She was born and raised in that valley, and buried and mourned there too, as the stone has it, in that order.
example_3: Put on your shoes and socks, hollered the coach, and the team knew what he meant.

definition: Fixed expressions whose meaning can't be assembled from the individual words.
example_1: He let the cat out of the bag before the invitations went out.
example_2: We're all ears — the meeting can't start without your story.
example_3: That printer costs an arm and a leg to feed.

definition: Language aimed at the senses — sight, sound, smell, taste, touch — to make a scene present.
example_1: Diesel and cinnamon tangled in the ferry terminal air.
example_2: Frost stitched white ferns across the window by morning.
example_3: The mango's juice ran sticky down to her elbow.

definition: Beginning the story in the middle of the action, with context filled in later.
example_1: The story opens with her halfway out the museum window, holding a fern that is not hers.
example_2: Page one: the wedding cake is already on the ferry, and the ferry is already leaving, and the groom is already swimming.
example_3: We meet the narrator mid-plummet, negotiating with a parachute he has just met.

definition: An indirect remark that suggests more than it says.
example_1: Lovely watch, said the pawnbroker. Your third this month.
example_2: The minutes note that refreshments vanished at a rate inconsistent with attendance.
example_3: Nice weather for repainting a boat, said the harbormaster, eyeing the very green hull that had been blue on Tuesday.

definition: An extended, ordered presentation of a character's private thoughts.
example_1: Through the whole handshake he inventoried it: too firm, overcorrected, now too long, abort, compliment the lobby.
example_2: As the recital began she ran the list again: bow, breathe, second ending not the first, and whatever happens, finish.
example_3: He watched the ferry dock and thought it through: one bag, two goodbyes, three reasons to stay, none of them load-bearing.

definition: Rhyme occurring within a single line, or between the middle and end of lines.
example_1: I found a mouse inside the house of cards we built.
example_2: The night was bright with satellite light.
example_3: She'd wait by the gate till the freight ran late.

definition: A sustained, vehement verbal attack on a target.
example_1: The columnist devoted eight hundred words to the intersection's new traffic pattern, calling it a monument to spite drawn with a broken crayon.
example_2: Her letter to the printer manufacturer opened politely and then went to sea: this machine is a paper-eating liar with the work ethic of fog.
example_3: The review of the folding tent ran two pages, the kindest phrase being 'origami betrayal.'

definition: Reversing customary syntactic order of subject, verb, or object — the umbrella term for flipped word order.
example_1: Came the winter, went the geese.
example_2: Rarely have leftovers caused such joy.
example_3: Down the hall marched the toddler, triumphant.

definition: A formal opening call to a muse or power for help with the telling.
example_1: Sing, spirit of the county fair, of funnel cakes and of the goat that got loose.
example_2: O muse of Monday mornings, lend me strength to describe this inbox.
example_3: Spirit of the tides, steady my pen while I tell how the ferry raced the storm.

definition: A gap between what is said or expected and what actually is — verbal, situational, or dramatic.
example_1: The fire station's smoke detector had dead batteries.
example_2: 'Lovely weather,' he said, wringing out his shoes.
example_3: We watch the babysitter praise the quiet while the kids paint the dog.

definition: Successive phrases or clauses built with the same length and structure.
example_1: Pack light, walk far, complain never.
example_2: The stew demands patience; the bread demands courage; the timing demands luck.
example_3: She came for the paycheck, stayed for the people, left for the mountains.

definition: Specialist vocabulary used to signal expertise, characterize a speaker, or fence outsiders out.
example_1: The barista asked if I wanted my pour-over as a single-origin washed-process with a extended bloom, and I said yes to whichever was coffee.
example_2: Grandma's quilting circle discussed fat quarters, feed dogs, and stitching in the ditch until the new member quietly googled under the table.
example_3: The climbing guide's report said the crux went at a soft 5.9 with bomber gear, which reassured exactly the people it was meant to.

definition: Placing two unlike things side by side so each sharpens the other.
example_1: Wedding photos taped inside the demolition permit.
example_2: A tank parked beside a lemonade stand.
example_3: The obituary ran next to the birth announcements, same font.

definition: Compound, metaphorical stand-ins for ordinary nouns, in the Old Norse style.
example_1: The sea kept its old name: whale-road.
example_2: He called the library a word-hoard and the librarian its dragon.
example_3: Sky-candle rose; the commute began.

definition: Deliberately repeating a key word throughout a narrative so it accumulates meaning.
example_1: The word 'ripe' returns in every chapter of the orchard novel, first for fruit, then for plans, finally for grief.
example_2: Across the story of the move, 'boxes' shifts from cardboard to burdens to, in the last line, gifts.
example_3: The memoir leans on 'tide' until the word means mother, schedule, and forgiveness all at once.

definition: A composition that deliberately avoids one letter of the alphabet.
example_1: For the contest she wrote a full page about picnics without using the letter e, and the crowd found it flawless.
example_2: His thank-you note skipped every o, a private joke for the aunt who taught him crosswords.
example_3: The classroom challenge: describe your summer without the letter a. The winner wrote about June, July, then 'the ninth month.'

definition: Affirming something by negating its opposite — understatement with a double negative.
example_1: The brakes were not unhelpful on that hill.
example_2: She's no stranger to a deadline.
example_3: It was not the worst wedding cake ever served.

definition: An object everyone in the story chases, whose actual nature barely matters.
example_1: Three families, one estate sale, and a locked recipe box nobody has opened; the plot never says what the recipe is.
example_2: The spies cross four borders for the briefcase, and the film ends before anyone looks inside.
example_3: Every pirate in the tale wants the brass compass that points, as far as the reader ever learns, nowhere in particular.

definition: Treating magical events as ordinary facts of an otherwise realistic world.
example_1: The bakery's bread rose only when the baker was forgiven, so the town kept short accounts.
example_2: Every Tuesday the grandmother floated an inch off the kitchen floor, and the family simply set her tea on the higher shelf.
example_3: Nobody remarked on the lake returning people's lost keys, though the ferry schedule did allow ten minutes for it.

definition: Comically swapping a word for a similar-sounding wrong one.
example_1: He's the very pineapple of politeness.
example_2: She called it a 'monumental erection of injustice' and meant 'edifice.'
example_3: Our team needs more social media exposure — we're practically incognito.

definition: Naming two contrasting parts of something to mean the whole of it.
example_1: We searched high and low for the ferry tickets, then found them in the guidebook.
example_2: Come rain or shine, the market opens at six.
example_3: She knew the trail root and ridge, and the trail knew her boots.

definition: Repeating the same word or phrase in the middle of successive clauses.
example_1: One paddle for the current, one paddle for the wind, one paddle for whatever the lake is planning.
example_2: We work through frost, we work through mud, we work through the foreman's harmonica.
example_3: Save some for the trip, save some for the toll, save some for the story after.

definition: Fiction that draws attention to its own status as a made-up story.
example_1: The detective complained that the author kept adding suspects whenever chapters ran short.
example_2: Footnote 12 apologizes for the weather in chapter 4, which the narrator admits was chosen purely for mood.
example_3: The novel's last page is a form the reader must sign, accepting delivery of one ending, as is.

definition: Calling one thing another to transfer its qualities, without 'like' or 'as.'
example_1: Deadlines are weather; bring a coat.
example_2: Her patience was a candle in a drafty room.
example_3: The spreadsheet is a garden of tiny locked doors.

definition: Referring to a thing by something closely associated with it.
example_1: The crown taxed the harbor; the harbor grumbled.
example_2: Hollywood loves a comeback.
example_3: The kitchen sent its compliments to table nine.

definition: Combining two incompatible metaphors, usually for comic effect.
example_1: We'll burn that bridge when we come to it.
example_2: The new manager promised to grab the bull by the horns and ride it to the moon.
example_3: Let's not count our chickens before they leave the station.

definition: Applying grand epic style to a trivial subject for comedy.
example_1: Arm yourself, O vacuum, for the syllabus of crumbs that awaits beneath the high chair.
example_2: The saga of the thermostat war spanned three floors, two dynasties of sticky notes, and one fallen space heater.
example_3: Of the great backyard mosquito campaign, let the ballads say: we lit the citronella, and it availed us nothing.

definition: A misheard phrase or lyric that produces an accidental new meaning.
example_1: For years she sang the anthem's line as 'grand mother waves of grain' and pictured her own.
example_2: The toddler reported that the song said 'olive, the other reindeer,' and named an actual olive.
example_3: He heard the ferry announcement as 'all passengers must wear a duck' and looked around for compliance.

definition: The atmosphere a text builds in the reader — the emotional weather of the piece.
example_1: Unwashed windows, a stopped clock, mail piled like snowdrift: the house felt paused.
example_2: String lights and frying onions made the alley feel like a holiday.
example_3: Every hallway in the report smelled faintly of bleach and secrets.

definition: A recurring image, phrase, or idea that accumulates meaning across a work.
example_1: Keys keep appearing — found, copied, swallowed — until the last door.
example_2: Every chapter opens with a weather report that is never right.
example_3: Someone is always sweeping in the background of this family's story.

definition: Telling the same events through several characters' viewpoints.
example_1: The fender bender occupies three chapters: the driver's, the cyclist's, and the extremely confident parrot witness's.
example_2: The wedding is told four times, and only the caterer's version explains the empty cake stand.
example_3: Each sibling narrates the storm from a different room, and the house only makes sense when the versions overlap.

definition: An opening engineered to seize the reader's attention immediately.
example_1: The first sentence: on the morning the lake vanished, my sister finally answered her phone.
example_2: The novel opens with a wedding invitation addressed to someone who has been missing for nine years.
example_3: Page one begins mid-inventory: four life jackets, three passports, one goat, no plan.

definition: The capacity to dwell in uncertainty and mystery without forcing a tidy answer — Keats's term.
example_1: The story never explains the light in the orchard, and is better for it.
example_2: She ends the memoir unsure whether her mother forgave her, and lets that stand.
example_3: The poem holds both grief and relief without breaking the tie.

definition: The agent of deserved downfall — the force that answers a character's offenses.
example_1: The inspector he bribed in chapter two signs the final report.
example_2: Her old apprentice, fired unfairly, returns owning the building.
example_3: For the speeding baron, the village pothole waited years.

definition: A newly coined word invented to name something existing words miss.
example_1: The family calls the pre-trip panic sweep of the house a 'leavening.'
example_2: She coined 'susurrus-hour' for the moment the campground goes quiet except for tents breathing.
example_3: The office invented 'meetingitis,' the ailment of calendars, and the diagnosis stuck.

definition: A statement that comically fails to follow from what came before.
example_1: We should repaint the fence, said Ida. Penguins can't taste sweetness, her brother replied.
example_2: The committee reviewed the drainage report, and Carl announced his uncle once met a llama with a passport photo.
example_3: Asked whether the bridge would hold, the contractor said he had always admired the accordion.

definition: An all-knowing narrator with access to every character's thoughts and every corner of the story.
example_1: The narrator tells us the bride's doubts, the caterer's triumph, and the pigeon's plans for the cake, all in one page.
example_2: While the twins argue over the map, the narration calmly notes that both are wrong and that the storm is early.
example_3: The story drifts from the ticket clerk's daydream to the conductor's secret to the ferry's slow rust, missing nothing.

definition: Words that imitate the sounds they name.
example_1: The screen door thwacked; the bees thrummed on.
example_2: Gravel crunched, then the kettle hissed its warning.
example_3: Plink, plink, plonk — the roof leak found the soup pot.

definition: Two contradictory words fused into one expression.
example_1: The manual offered clear confusion in four languages.
example_2: They served jumbo shrimp at the tiny banquet.
example_3: It was an open secret and a working vacation.

definition: A word or phrase that reads the same backward as forward.
example_1: They named the twin kayaks Kayak One and Kayak Two, honoring a word that paddles the same both ways.
example_2: Her civic pride was literal: she loved that 'civic' mirrored itself like the town square's fountain.
example_3: At noon, he noted, even the clock's word for it reads the same coming and going.

definition: A short story about ordinary people that teaches a moral or spiritual lesson.
example_1: A woman lent her ladder to every neighbor but never climbed it herself, until harvest, when every orchard in town sent back apples.
example_2: Two brothers split a field; the one who fenced first spent his life mending, the other spent it planting.
example_3: The parable of the borrowed umbrella: it kept the borrower dry, and the lender learned who ran toward rain.

definition: Reframing a fault as a virtue by renaming it generously.
example_1: He is not cheap; he is a curator of the free.
example_2: She's not lost; she is aggressively scenic.
example_3: The toddler isn't stubborn; he has executive presence.

definition: A statement that contradicts itself yet points at a truth.
example_1: The faster she saved time, the less of it she had.
example_2: You must know the rules well to break them well.
example_3: The emptiest calendar felt the heaviest.

definition: Using the same grammatical structure across related phrases so they balance.
example_1: We came for the harvest, we stayed for the dance, we left with the recipes.
example_2: Measure the door, mark the hinge, trust the level.
example_3: What the tide takes slowly, the storm takes at once.

definition: A sentence whose ending swerves to force a surprised rereading of the start.
example_1: She has a heart of gold, appraised and in a vault.
example_2: I childproofed the whole house, and yet they keep getting in.
example_3: The camping trip brought us closer together, mostly around 3 a.m., in one collapsed tent.

definition: Setting short clauses side by side without subordinating one to another.
example_1: The tide came in. The sandcastle voted to remain. The vote failed.
example_2: Dawn broke. The rooster took full credit. Nobody argued.
example_3: We packed. The car refused. We unpacked. The porch approved.

definition: Inserting an aside into the middle of a sentence as an interruption.
example_1: The chili (a family recipe, which is to say a family argument) won second place.
example_2: Our guide, who had (he mentioned twice) summited actual mountains, lost us in the gift shop.
example_3: The invoice included a fee for expedited shipping (the package walked, apparently, and took scenic routes).

definition: Imitating a familiar style or form to poke fun at it.
example_1: The camp newsletter ran nature documentary narration for the lost-sock bin: here, in the dim understory, the single sock waits for a mate that will never come.
example_2: Her toast was a weather forecast for the marriage: patchy bickering clearing by evening, sustained warmth, chance of casseroles.
example_3: The kids rewrote the fire-drill instructions as a cooking show: today we are evacuating calmly, single file, to a crisp golden parking lot.

definition: Conceding a minor point in order to strengthen your larger argument.
example_1: Yes, the canoe leaks; it also holds six crates more than your truck can.
example_2: Granted, the recipe takes all day. That is the argument for it.
example_3: Fine, the shortcut adds a hill. It subtracts the highway, the toll, and your uncle's commentary.

definition: An affectionate imitation or blend of another style, without mockery.
example_1: The anniversary card was written as a hard-boiled detective report: she walked into my life like trouble with a library card.
example_2: His birthday poem for the dog borrowed the cadence of old sea shanties, all haul and heave and biscuit.
example_3: The bakery menu is a loving imitation of epic catalogs: of flour, of butter, of the seven braided glories.

definition: Nature or objects mirroring human emotion — the weather grieves with the widow.
example_1: The sky sulked gray through the whole custody hearing.
example_2: On acceptance day, even the potholes seemed to grin.
example_3: The wind wailed over the auction of the farm.

definition: Appealing directly to the audience's emotions to move them.
example_1: The shelter's flyer says only: he waits by the door at six, because someone used to come home at six.
example_2: The last stall at the market held one crate of apples and a sign: my final harvest, forty good years, thank you.
example_3: Donate a coat, the poster asked, because recess does not check the thermometer.

definition: A sentence that withholds its main clause until the end, building suspense.
example_1: After the flood, after the forms, after the third inspector, the house was ours.
example_2: Though the map lied and the mule quit, though the pass froze, we crossed.
example_3: Whatever the neighbors say, whatever the record shows, she paid.

definition: A sudden reversal of a character's fortunes, from good to bad or bad to good.
example_1: The bakery's grand reopening was interrupted by the health inspector, who had come, it turned out, to deliver a wholesale contract.
example_2: One paragraph after winning the regatta, she watched the prize boat drift off with the tide and her keys.
example_3: The understudy learned two things at intermission: the lead had recovered, and the lead had recovered his singing voice, not his memory of act two.

definition: Roundabout phrasing that uses more words than needed, often for effect or evasion.
example_1: He is a person to whom punctuality remains a distant acquaintance.
example_2: The device for the summoning of elevators had ceased its labors.
example_3: She achieved a state of non-employment by mutual agreement.

definition: Writing in the adopted voice of an invented character distinct from the author.
example_1: For the whole column, the food critic writes as the town's crankiest seagull, reviewing wharfs by chip availability.
example_2: Her poems are all spoken by a retired carousel horse with strong opinions about circles.
example_3: The gardening blog's narrator is an immortal groundhog who signs every post 'your adversary, respectfully.'

definition: Granting human qualities to abstractions or objects figuratively, in a phrase or image.
example_1: Doubt pulled up a chair and ordered coffee.
example_2: The deadline leaned on the doorbell.
example_3: Autumn signed its name across the parking lot.

definition: Using redundant words for emphasis or flavor.
example_1: I heard it with my own ears, in person, live.
example_2: The end result was a small little cabin, built by hand by human hands.
example_3: Let me repeat myself again: the free gift costs nothing.

definition: The arranged sequence of causally linked events — what happens, in the order the story tells it.
example_1: Girl finds ledger; ledger names uncle; dinner becomes trial.
example_2: A stolen bike, a wrong pawnshop, a right friendship, in that order.
example_3: The will is read first; the funeral, suspiciously, comes later.

definition: An unexpected development that reframes what the story seemed to be.
example_1: The inheritance dispute ends when the notary reveals the cottage was never the grandmother's to leave; she was its tenant, and the will names her landlord: the cat.
example_2: In the final chapter, the anonymous donor funding the lighthouse repairs signs the last check with the keeper's own name.
example_3: The detective gathers everyone to name the thief, and the painting walks in, returned by the forger who could not stand the frame.

definition: An outcome where virtue is rewarded and wrongdoing punished with pointed fittingness.
example_1: The neighbor who hoarded the shared hose spent August watching his own lawn burn out from behind a locked shed.
example_2: She gave her bus seat away every morning for years; the retirement raffle's grand prize was a reserved seat with her name stitched on it.
example_3: The critic who mocked the community garden was assigned, by lottery, its only shadeless plot, and the tomatoes forgave him slowly.

definition: The narrative position from which a story is told — first, second, third limited, omniscient.
example_1: The heist retold by the getaway driver's 'I' hides half the plan.
example_2: A recipe narrated as 'you' turns dinner into a dare.
example_3: An all-seeing narrator pities both armies and spoils neither.

definition: Repeating words that share a root but appear in different forms.
example_1: The judge judged the judging harshly.
example_2: Choose carefully, chooser; choices choose back.
example_3: The builder built what the buildable lot allowed, and the building agreed.

definition: Piling on conjunctions between items to slow and swell the rhythm.
example_1: We hauled water and wood and rope and doubt up the hill.
example_2: The fair had lights and mud and fiddles and rain and nobody left.
example_3: He apologized and explained and promised and, finally, listened.

definition: A new word blending the sounds and meanings of two others.
example_1: Breakfast plus lunch became brunch and claimed Sunday.
example_2: The hotel's 'workcation' package included a desk with an ocean view.
example_3: Their spork policy ended the fork budget crisis.

definition: A time-loop plot in which the attempt to prevent an event is what causes it.
example_1: He traveled back to stop the barn fire, and his dropped lantern is in every history of it.
example_2: The warning note she sent to her younger self was the very note that made her take the ferry.
example_3: The inventor destroyed the blueprints to keep the machine from existing, and the shredded pieces taught his apprentice how it worked.

definition: A list of alternatives set up as foils before pivoting to the real subject of praise.
example_1: Some love the mountains, some the open sea, some the roar of cities; give me the porch, the rain, and a working thermos.
example_2: Others collect coins, or stamps, or vintage spoons; my grandmother collected exits from boring conversations.
example_3: Let some praise sunrise runs and some praise midnight trains; I praise the nap, undefeated champion of afternoons.

definition: Raising a likely objection yourself so you can answer it on your own terms.
example_1: You will say the boat is too old. The barnacles say otherwise; they have signed a long lease.
example_2: Some will object that a goat cannot be mayor. To them I say: read the town charter, which is silent on hooves.
example_3: Of course you'll ask about the cost. The roof answers that question every time it rains.

definition: An opening section before the main narrative that frames or precedes it.
example_1: A burned page dated forty years earlier opens the mystery.
example_2: Before chapter one, the lighthouse keeper explains why the log is missing.
example_3: The play begins with a chorus promising two hours and one shipwreck.

definition: Wordplay exploiting words with multiple meanings or similar sounds.
example_1: The cheese shop's slogan: brie yourself.
example_2: I used to be a banker, but I lost interest.
example_3: Broken pencils are pointless, said the stationery store sign.

definition: A misleading clue planted to draw attention away from the truth.
example_1: The muddy boots by the door belonged, three chapters later, to the plumber, as the detective finally admits.
example_2: The mystery dwells on the butler's locked trunk, which holds nothing but his prize-winning jam recipes.
example_3: Every suspicion points at the new neighbor with the covered truck, who turns out to be delivering pianos to the church.

definition: Refuting an idea by extending its logic to an absurd conclusion.
example_1: If we cancel recess whenever it drizzles, we should also cancel lunch whenever someone is hungry.
example_2: By the committee's logic, since one goose was rude, we must now ban the sky.
example_3: Sure, skip the oil change to save money; skip enough of them and you'll save on the whole concept of a car.

definition: A line or phrase repeated at intervals throughout a piece.
example_1: Between every verse about the harvest, the song returns: but the rain knows the schedule.
example_2: Each family story that night ended the same way: and that is why we measure twice.
example_3: The poem circles back after every stanza to the ferry horn, the ferry horn, until the reader hears it too.

definition: A rapid exchange of witty remarks between speakers.
example_1: Nice of you to be early for once. I'm late for tomorrow, actually.
example_2: This soup needs something. A eulogy, offered her brother, ladling seconds.
example_3: You fish like a poet. Fine, then you cook like a fisherman, and neither of us is eating tonight.

definition: Telling a story backward, from ending toward beginning.
example_1: The novel opens with the sold sign on the farmhouse and closes, two hundred pages earlier, with the first seed going in.
example_2: First we see the trophy in the attic box, then the championship, then the tryout she almost skipped.
example_3: The story starts at the divorce of the business partners and rewinds to the lemonade stand where it all began.

definition: A question asked for effect, with no answer expected.
example_1: Who among us has ever folded a fitted sheet on the first try?
example_2: Is the dog going to walk himself?
example_3: What harbor ever complained about a lighthouse?

definition: The ordered pattern of end rhymes in a stanza, mapped with letters like ABAB.
example_1: The postcard poem ran ABAB: shore, light, door, night.
example_2: Limericks strut their AABBA and dare you to finish one politely.
example_3: Her sonnet held ABAB CDCD EFEF GG, tidy as a packed suitcase.

definition: The combined beat of stressed syllables and the chime of matching sounds that give verse its music.
example_1: The jump-rope chant swung steady: two beats, slap, repeat.
example_2: Read aloud, the couplet rocked like oars: dip and pull, dip and pull.
example_3: The jingle stuck because the drum of it matched the ding of it.

definition: Pointed verbal irony intended to cut, saying the opposite of what is meant.
example_1: Oh sure, park the kayak in the kitchen; that is exactly what kitchens are for.
example_2: Great idea, testing the smoke alarm at midnight; the neighbors were dying to be involved.
example_3: No, please, tell me more about the shortcut while we admire this cornfield from inside it.

definition: Using humor, exaggeration, or ridicule to expose folly in people, institutions, or customs.
example_1: A mock catalog sells 'artisanal tap water' to the neighborhood that closed the well.
example_2: The office memo praises synergy while the building lacks chairs.
example_3: Swift proposed eating babies to shame a policy that starved them.

definition: Stacking a series of near-synonymous words or phrases to hammer one idea.
example_1: The trail was a slog, a grind, a march, a long argument with gravity.
example_2: Her desk was chaos, clutter, a landfill with a lamp.
example_3: The referee's call: final, settled, done, carved in whistle.

definition: Narrating with 'you' as the protagonist, placing the reader inside the story.
example_1: You take the night shift at the toll booth because the stars are free there, and by June you know every trucker's wave.
example_2: You promise yourself one row of the quilt before bed. The clock, you notice later, has given up on you.
example_3: You board the ferry with the last box of your old apartment and let the wake do the talking.

definition: A prediction that comes true because it was made.
example_1: Certain the bridge club would exclude her, she skipped every meeting, and the empty chair became her proof.
example_2: The forecast of a sugar shortage sent the whole town hoarding, and by Friday the shelves proved the rumor right.
example_3: Told he would fumble, the rookie thought only of fumbling, and his hands obliged.

definition: The time and place a story inhabits, and the texture of that world.
example_1: A border-town laundromat during the hottest August on record.
example_2: The story never leaves the overnight ferry between two feuding islands.
example_3: A basement archive in 1979, lit by one honest bulb.

definition: Clustering s and sh sounds so a passage hisses and hushes.
example_1: Soft surf sifted seashells across the silver shallows.
example_2: The chestnuts hissed as steam whispered past the roaster's shovel.
example_3: She shushed the restless spaniels as snow slid, whispering, from the cedars.

definition: A comparison using 'like' or 'as.'
example_1: The apology arrived like a plumber — late and expensive.
example_2: Her focus was as narrow as a keyhole.
example_3: The rumor moved like grease on a hot pan.

definition: A near-rhyme pairing words with similar but not identical sounds.
example_1: Her couplet leaned 'lantern' against 'return,' and the almost-match glowed.
example_2: The song rhymes 'harbor' with 'over,' close enough for the tide.
example_3: He paired 'shovel' with 'gravel' and let the grit of the near-miss do the work.

definition: A speech in which a character, alone, thinks aloud.
example_1: Alone in the walk-in cooler, the chef weighed the offer out loud, shelf by shelf: new city, new kitchen, same hands.
example_2: The night watchman paced the museum arguing with himself about the letter in his pocket, and the statues kept his counsel.
example_3: Left with the seedlings, she rehearsed both sides of the decision until the greenhouse fogged.

definition: Swapping the initial sounds of nearby words, usually to comic effect.
example_1: She toasted the 'queer old dean' instead of the dear old queen.
example_2: He offered a 'lack of pies' when he meant a pack of lies.
example_3: Our choir sang 'the Lord is a shoving leopard.'

definition: A grouped set of lines in a poem, set off by space — poetry's paragraph.
example_1: The hymn moved in four-line rooms, each with its own window.
example_2: Her elegy used couplets: two lines, a held breath, repeat.
example_3: The last stanza stood alone, one line long, like a door closing.

definition: Dialogue that alternates in rapid single lines, thrust and parry.
example_1: Sell the boat. Buy a boat? Sell it. It's the house's boat. The house says sell.
example_2: You're late. The bridge was up. The bridge lies. The bridge and I agree on nothing else.
example_3: Did you knock? Twice. Loudly? Politely. That explains the year of silence.

definition: A narrative embedded inside another narrative.
example_1: During the blackout, the babysitter tells the kids a tale about a babysitter telling tales, and the candles do the rest.
example_2: Halfway through the road trip novel, a hitchhiker recounts a whole second novel about the same highway, told from the ditch.
example_3: The play pauses while the innkeeper performs the legend of the inn, and the audience watches both stories check in.

definition: Narration that follows the unfiltered flow of a mind — associative, unpunctuated by logic.
example_1: Buy stamps why do they still exist mother's birthday the ninth no the tenth stamps.
example_2: The whole exam hour is one unbroken sentence about the proctor's squeaking shoe.
example_3: Joyce lets Bloom's lunch thoughts wander from soap to funerals to cheese.

definition: The engineered tension of waiting to learn what happens.
example_1: The elevator stops between floors; the narrator counts the breaths.
example_2: We know the visa expires Friday; the chapter is dated Thursday.
example_3: Every ring of the phone in that house lands like a struck match.

definition: A two-premise argument that marches to a conclusion, useful straight or for comedy.
example_1: All ferries wait for no one; I am no one; therefore the ferry will wait for me, reasoned the late passenger, incorrectly.
example_2: Everything Grandma bakes wins ribbons. This pie is Grandma's. Clear a shelf.
example_3: Muddy dogs get baths. The dog can hear the word bath. Therefore the dog is now a rumor under the porch.

definition: A concrete thing that carries a meaning beyond itself.
example_1: The spare house key, never reclaimed, said the marriage was over.
example_2: A jar of hometown dirt rode every tour bus with him.
example_3: The community garden's one sunflower outgrew the fence and the argument.

definition: Repeating one phrase at the start and another at the end of successive clauses, combining anaphora and epistrophe.
example_1: When the well ran dry, we hauled together. When the barn went up, we hauled together.
